title: The Baby in Vevey Who Led Henri Nestlé to Stake Everything
dek: In 1867 a struggling Vevey manufacturer tried his milk-and-bread infant food on a premature baby nobody expected to live, then put everything into it.

story.event: Developing an infant food in 1867 and committing his business to it after a premature baby recovered
story.summary: In 1867 Henri Nestlé, a German-born manufacturer in Vevey whose street-gas business had lost its market, developed an infant food from milk, wheat flour and sugar, following Liebig's 1865 analysis of breast milk with a simpler process. After a premature baby who could not take breast milk or the usual substitutes recovered on it, he and his wife put all their money and energy into the product and set up a factory within months. Output rose from 8,600 tins in 1868 to more than a million in 1875, when he sold the business.
paragraphs: In 1867 Henri Nestlé was 53, a German-born pharmacist's assistant turned manufacturer in Vevey, on Lake Geneva, and his business needed a future. Since 1843 he had made and sold oil, bone meal, vinegar, liqueurs, mineral water and fertiliser, and from 1858 to 1862 he had supplied gas for the town's street lamps. Then his partner ran into money trouble and Vevey moved to a coal-gas works. His biographer, the historian Albert Pfiffner, writes that the search for a new main income led him to an unsolved problem: feeding babies who could not be breastfed.

Infant mortality was high, and the substitutes on offer were complicated to prepare. Nestlé's own first attempts had not gone well. When the chemist Justus von Liebig published an analysis of breast milk in 1865, with a correct but laborious recipe, Nestlé went back to his laboratory. His food used the same main ingredients as most rivals, milk, wheat flour and sugar, but a different process: sweetened milk thickened under vacuum, mixed with powdered, baked wheat bread, then dried and ground. Parents only had to boil it with water. He wrote that it was not a new discovery, just a sound and rational use of ingredients long known to suit infants.

That year a premature baby in Vevey who could not keep down his mother's milk or any usual substitute, and was not expected to live, was given a diluted version. He recovered. Pfiffner writes that this unexpected success persuaded Nestlé and his wife, Clémentine, to put all their energy and money into the new product, and within months they had a factory making it. Nestlé stopped his other lines and sent samples to doctors, pharmacists and hospitals around Europe. The orders, he said later, came like avalanches.

The factory made 8,600 tins in 1868 and more than a million in 1875, by which time the food was sold in 18 countries under a bird's-nest emblem taken from his family's coat of arms. The couple had no children, and the plant took nearly every hour they had. In 1875, at 61, Nestlé sold the business for a million francs, writing to a friend that he needed rest, and his wife no less.

quote.text: Such services formed a part of the Zen discipline and every least action must be done absolutely perfectly. Thus many a weighty discussion ensued while weeding the garden, paring a turnip, or serving tea.
quote.source_title: The Book of Tea, Project Gutenberg eBook #769
quote.connection: Nestlé claimed no new discovery, only familiar ingredients handled properly enough that a worried parent could use them. Okakura describes monks who treated paring a turnip as seriously as doctrine. Both place the worth of a thing in the care given to ordinary materials rather than in their novelty.

reflection: It is easy to believe that work only counts if it is new. Nestlé said plainly that his was not: milk, bread and sugar, which everyone knew, made in a way a tired parent could actually manage. The value was in the handling.

Much of what you do is like that, things already known, done carefully for someone who needs them done right. The end of the story belongs to it too. After eight years Nestlé wrote that he and his wife needed rest, and he took it. Knowing when you have given enough is part of doing a thing well.
invitation: Pick one ordinary task on today's list and decide, before you start, what doing it properly would mean. Do it to that standard, and then let it be finished.

research_notes: The story keeps to 1867-1875 and does not discuss the company's later history. The baby: House of Switzerland calls him a days-old infant, Nestlé's own pages a premature infant who could not take his mother's milk or conventional substitutes, and Börse Online (2019) a boy named Jules, born a month early, who had refused other food for weeks and recovered in October 1867, adding that Nestlé took him into his own house; the NDB says only 'a sick infant'. Because the age and the home-care detail are not corroborated, the story says only that a premature baby who could not keep down breast milk or substitutes, and was not expected to live, was given a diluted version and recovered, and does not name him. Whether the trial came before or after the first sales is unclear (House of Switzerland says 'during the trial phase'; Nestlé CWA describes it after the launch), so the story says 'that year'. Output: House of Switzerland and Börse Online give 8,600 tins in 1868, 670,000 in 1874 and over a million in 1875; Nestlé CWA dates the 8,600 to autumn 1867; the NDB says over a million tins after seven years. The story uses 1868 and 1875. Nestlé's own words are paraphrased, not quoted, because they reach us only in German translation (Börse Online): that his invention was not a new discovery but a rational use of long-known ingredients, that orders came 'like avalanches', and that he needed rest 'and my wife no less'. Character: House of Switzerland calls him unafraid of risk; Pfiffner in the NDB calls him cautious rather than a risk-taker; the story avoids either label. The NDB article, by Albert Pfiffner, lists the Nestlé archive in Vevey and the Vevey communal archives among its sources; the NDB is an edited national biography. The Nestlé company pages block automated requests and are cited from Internet Archive copies. The Okakura passage describes the duties of Zen monks and is applied by analogy.
